s1.explanation: The unit responds to a close, front-facing face of a furry mammal such as a fox, cat, lynx, red panda or papillon. It is most active when both eyes look at the camera, the upright ears are visible and the head is large in the frame. Fox-like orange or reddish fur helps further. Activity drops sharply when the face is hidden (eating, curled up asleep, hanging upside down), seen in profile, or small and distant in the scene. This face dependence is what separates it from similar units, which stay active on hidden-face cats and foxes.

s3.explanation: Responds to the face of a furry mammal (fox, cat, lynx, red panda, small dog) seen from the front and looking toward the camera, with both eyes and erect pointed ears visible, especially when the head is large in the frame. Activity is strongest for orange or ginger faces with white markings, such as a fox staring at the camera or a red panda. Activity is weak when the face is hidden, turned to profile, buried (eating, curled up asleep), or small and distant. The similar units stay active on these hidden-face or distant photos, which this unit does not.

s2.explanation: The unit responds to a close, front-facing face of a furry mammal (fox, red panda, lynx, cat, papillon) with both eyes open and looking toward the camera, and upright pointed ears framing it. Orange or ginger fur with white face markings helps. Activity drops sharply when the face is hidden (eating, curled up, hanging away), turned to a profile, has closed eyes, or is small and distant in the frame. Similar units still respond to these hidden-face or body-only photos, so the visible open-eyed frontal face is what is particular to this unit.
